High dynamic range photography enables capturing scenes with significant differences in brightness. Traditional high dynamic range photography involves taking photographs at various exposure levels and merging them. Determining different exposure settings, absent in smartphone cameras that lack this feature, is our focus in this paper. We present an optimized approach to selecting exposure settings by formulating this problem as a linear program, considering luminance constraints, image noise characteristics, and human perception of human visual system. Our proposed solution outperforms existing methods in terms of reconstructed image quality. By training deep neural networks to evaluate image reconstruction results, this can be efficiently executed on mobile devices within less than one second per image.

Artificial Neural Networks are advancing rapidly, with their intricate inner workings being compared to a causal system. This paper aims to provide the first comprehensive framework that maps the connections between various aspects of an Artifiicial Neural Network to its corresponding components in a Causal Model. This framework will enable targeted interventions on specific parts of the network, facilitating both a deeper understanding of the network's inner mechanisms and the facilitation of neural network optimization processes. Through rigorous mathematical derivations, we have established direct correlations between the Causal Model and the Neural Network, thereby offering a means to optimize neural network optimization processes. We have also demonstrated the framework's effectiveness in several neural network optimization scenarios, including the isolation of influences between entities, the isolation of causes from effects, the separation of data from concepts, and the acceleration of the training process.

Understanding how heat moves through the packed bed is essential for many chemical engineering processes.  However, measuring the temperature within this environment remains a significant challenge.  Our research presents an innovative method to investigate heat distribution within a gas-solid bed by utilizing high-speed MRI in the presence of a localized heat source.  By applying high spatial and temporal resolution MRI, we were able to monitor the heat propagation as it entered and exited individual void spaces, while temperatures measured with pyrometers confirmed our MRI findings.  Moreover, our high-resolution data enabled the creation of detailed cross-sections showing the complex heat patterns formed as they navigate around solid particles, nematic heat lines, and regions of accumulated heat, all while the bed remains stationary.

In 1965, D Mumford hypothesized that for hyperbolic Riemann surfaces R of sufficiently high genus, the maximum area of a bibounded principle-compliant subset would converge to 4π as genus increases. We have formulated and analyzed a variant of this hypothesis, known as the b-principle for compact Riemann surfaces. Our research reveals a direct correlation between the maximum feeble b-principle-compliant area and the number of homology cycles in two dimensions that intersect in a single point.

This study focuses on the complex nature of cardiac mechanics simulations, which are essential for various applications in cardiac physiology and medicine. Despite their benefits, these simulations face significant challenges due to their high computational demands, particularly in postcardiovascular surgery when the heart's geometry and material properties vary widely. To address this issue, the research investigates the use of coupled level-set and finite element methods in combination with advanced coupling schemes and multilevel multilocal tensor product solvers. Through a comprehensive multibody simulation of a heart-graft, multiple preconditioners were tested, utilizing distinct solvers, multigrid techniques, and patch methods. By assessing the balance between their individual efficiencies, the study found that the proposed scalable multilevel multilocal tensor product solver offers improved performance over traditional approaches, particularly in terms of balanced accuracy and solution time.

The traditional "random arrays" model involves generating independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) real numbers, organized in an $n \times n$ grid. This study expands on that framework by introducing an $n$-cell shape, also placed in an $n \times n$ grid, that grows at a comparable rate. This framework encompasses various well-known random matrices as well as non-crossing partitions, but encompasses a broader range. When the probability distribution of the grid numbers is standard normal, we examine the long-term behavior of the sum of the cells' numbers, normalized by an appropriate factor. This includes identifying universal limiting laws that mirror those found in random matrices, as well as non-i.i.d. settings. In addition, we explore boundary cases with distinct outcomes.

In recent years, Deep Learning's remarkable performance on visual and linguistic tasks has led to a rapid advancement in the development of video creation tools, which are now capable of producing high-quality, convincing videos through the collaborative use of text-based generation models and AI-generated audio and visual components. This survey explores the latest breakthroughs in AI-assisted video creation, covering end-to-end models as well as individually focused approaches, including narrative analysis, text-to-image generation, and lip synchronization. We outline common data sources, technical approaches, and evaluation metrics used to assess these methods, which can achieve a convincing output in videos. This survey can serve as a comprehensive reference for researchers and practitioners by providing an overview of the challenges and a roadmap for potential directions for improvement in AI-assisted video creation.

This work aims to counteract the overoptimism often exhibited by models toward their own performance. While some researchers have attempted to measure a model's confident mistakes through comparison with other models or human evaluators, these approaches do not scale effectively. In this study, we introduce a method to quantify a model's deceptive sense of safety in a controlled setting. By adapting the notions of margin and separation from our previous work on model sense, we evaluate the model's deceptive ability to distinguish between safe and unsafe actions. Our results demonstrate that LLMs exhibit a clear distinction between their safe and unsafe predictions, but this differs significantly from their general awareness. Moreover, we found that more capable models are more inclined to express doubt in situations that pose a safety risk. Our data is made available to facilitate future investigations into the deceptive nature of models' sense of safety.

Researchers have developed a pioneering class of acoustic devices called microacoustic metagratings, capable of managing remarkable ultra-high wavelength ultra-high-temperature sounds caused by molecular gases. These microacoustic metagratings, composed of intricate surface patterns etched onto solid materials, are designed to facilitate efficient heat transmission even in chloroform vapor, despite its hindered transmission. The decorative patterns of the microacoustic metagratings correspond to complex interference figures, with their peak depth and temperature stability exceeding those of standard grating structures. This exceptional performance is attributed to their robustness and consistency in accommodating different types of sounds. Furthermore, their precise dimensions, less than a hundred nanometers, enable them to manage extremely high-frequency sounds generated by hot gases. The demonstration of these properties is achieved through the use of chloroform vapor and chloroform vapor heated to extremely high temperatures.

In anomalous diffusion within random media, the mean squared displacement grows at a linear rate, but a significant fraction of particles exhibit displacement growth at a super-linear rate. A new metric, fractional RMS displacement, is introduced to better reflect the typical movement of particles. In a high-dimensional lattice model, a linear growth pattern is found to be directly related to the degree of dispersion and influenced by dimensionality. The study suggests that media with random properties, such as porosity, can lead to anomalous diffusion by drawing parallels to the movement of flowing substances, and the concept of FPMSD can aid in evaluating diffusion processes in various fields of study.

The study examines how linear and Kerr nonlinear interactions affect the mode coupling near the edge of a two-dimensional lattice, specifically in waveguides and enclosed resonators. Using a universal model, researchers analyzed the impact of sine and cubic term couplings on the system's dynamics. The analysis covers various geometries and the relative strengths of the linear and nonlinear term. The findings can be applied to a wide range of photonic systems and enable the study of complex phenomena such as discrete vortex liquids and droplets, and multicomponent topological fluids.

Lyapunov-based methods are extensively utilized in stability analysis and control design for nonlinear systems characterized by bounded controls. Nonetheless, these techniques are limited by this specific condition and cannot be applied to nonlinear systems that can be regulated by unbounded controls. This research extends the Lyapunov-based stability analysis and control synthesis theories to accommodate unbounded controls in general nonlinear systems. We present two key results: a Lyapunov theorem ensuring global asymptotic stability with convergent convergence rates, and an extension of the converse Lyapunov theorem for unbounded controls. Additionally, we establish a counterpart Barbalossa theorem for discontinuous functions. These findings are illustrated through their application to the infinite sliding mode in convex problems.

A new technique for restoring high-resolution details in turbulent flows has been proposed, utilizing a generative adversarial network (GAN) framework, specifically a spectral normalizing flow (S-NF) model.  To gather data for training, a direct numerical simulation (DNS) with limited resolution was conducted, followed by generating a corresponding high-resolution dataset through DNS at the same Reynolds number.  The S-NF model was then trained to convert the low-resolution dataset back to its high-resolution equivalent, and was evaluated against other downscaling methods using (inverse) energy cascades.  Despite utilizing only limited-resolution training data, the proposed S-NF approach successfully captured fine-scale details in turbulent kinetic energy spectra and two-point correlation functions, performing comparably to (stochastic) subgrid-scale modeling when assessing energy cascades.  Additionally, the results indicate that this technique can be successfully applied across a range of Reynolds numbers.

We suggest incorporating observables into the mathematical framework of the wave equation, which is commonly used to model light and other non-relativistic particles. This could potentially lead to a more intuitive, physics-centric interpretation of the equation's solution, in contrast to the prevailing practice of adding probabilistic elements externally. This approach may be especially useful for the particle version of the wave equation.

High-performance systems that operate at extreme temperatures are frequently utilized in demanding applications such as data centers, vehicles, and buildings, but these environments often suffer from thermal fluctuations due to changes in system energy, temperature, and environmental conditions. These variations can lead to open-world uncertainty about the boundaries of training data for machine learning models, which can negatively affect their performance and reliability. This issue poses a challenge for ensuring the systems' assurance, as current approaches based on confidence scores are inadequate for capturing this type of uncertainty. This paper introduces a novel method for exploring the relationship between energy and temperature variations and their impact on open-world uncertainty, which allows for the investigation of uncertainty boundaries and the development of score-based confidence measures. This approach is integrated into a novel method for ensuring the systems' assurance, which is demonstrated through comprehensive evaluations and best practice guidelines for effective assurance calibration.

Dynamic life-long learning is a crucial aspect of machine learning that is
essential in preparing for and achieving true generalization. However,
supervised reinforcement learning frameworks are typically confined to static
datasets that are intended for a specific period. These limited frameworks
are often evaluated using artificial reward functions and environments that
lacked complexity. To address this limitation, we have created a comprehensive
lifelong reinforcement learning evaluation framework known as L2Ex, which is
composed of multiple evaluation modules designed to test and evaluate various
aspects of reinforcement learning algorithms in complex environments. These
evaluation modules include: (i) redundant states, (ii) state sparsity, (iii)
transfer difficulty, (iv) unstructured data, and (v) continuous environments.
We have conducted in-depth analyses of various reinforcement learning algorithms
in our framework and found that they perform better in complex, dynamic
environments with lower redundancy and more efficient use of available states.
Moreover, we have observed that pretraining on smaller environments can
significantly improve the performance of agents when they are transferred to
more complex environments. The L2Ex framework is an important step towards
developing sophisticated, general-purpose reinforcement learning agents that
can excel even in our evaluation modules but also in a wide range of additional
real-world environments.

A significant issue in the current industry regarding business processes is the lack of robust, adaptable, and efficient monitoring methods based on declarative processes. To overcome this limitation, a novel approach based on declarative processes has been introduced, which involves three main components: a monitoring and testing method on process traces, a network-based exploration and learning system on processes, and the integration of these approaches through monitoring games. A key contribution of this approach is its use of infinite streams to more accurately and completely characterize processes, as opposed to the current focus on process traces. A formalism combining these aspects based on streams has been developed, which involves the concepts of monitoring games and proposals. To execute these approaches, a subsetting based on differential equations has been developed, which allows for the efficient computation of monitoring and testing outcomes on infinite streams, as well as the implementation of suggestions and processes. To demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, an equation to accelerate trace testing based on partial completion has been developed, as well as an approach to testing and completing partially completed traces using suggestions based on additional incomplete traces. Furthermore, the approach includes the concept of completeness, which refers to the ability to detect all relevant errors in the trace. To illustrate the approach, two examples have been provided, as well as the inclusion of required background information and a comprehensive summary of the approach.

In one-dimensional photonic quasicrystals, light propagation can exhibit a striking phenomenon where localized modes suddenly transition to quasi-extended modes at specific points, causing a abrupt rise in quasi-resonance widths and mode volumes, which we call the reentrant delocalization shift (RDSS). By employing a simple, large-unit-cell model and supporting it with experimental data from a tunable photonic quasicrystal waveguide, we show that the RDSS reentrant delocalization shift can be triggered when a quasi-extended RD mode coexists with strong local modes within the same energy band, increasing RD modes' ability to interact with their environment. Furthermore, we provide design principles for devices that rely on quasicrystalline photonics, taking advantage of the RDSS to achieve exceptional delocalized-local hybrid mode large interaction strengths.

Liger, a high-performance instrument with 141 detectors, is optimized for 1D and 2D spectroscopy at the Keck Observatory. It supports a wide wavelength range and has 101 x 400G interfaces, which are essential for handling the massive data output of 1D spectroscopy instruments and 2D spectroscopy instruments. Liger's software system includes the Data Processing Software, which is responsible for controlling the instrument, managingKeVO, and processing data. This software system is built on the framework of the Key Engineering Villard Observatory. This paper presents the development of Liger's data processing software, describes the features of the Liger instrument, and presents the challenges and solutions encountered during the development of the software system.

Quantifying the spatial distribution of two-photon entanglement in radial-Helical modes offers vital insight into the characteristics of spontaneous parametric down-conversion and the performance of holograms in mode conversion. Researchers have utilized spatial mode cameras to measure the radial-Helical spectrum of entangled photons by combining two single photon spectra in a specific way, but this method's resolution is limited due to the overlapping of spectral features. A new technique has been proposed to surpass the diffraction limit by incorporating a mathematical model of the spectral spectrum and the use of compressive sensing to analyze the spectral features of bi-photons in a two-dimensional plane. The method's effectiveness is demonstrated theoretically and experimentally, utilizing the spectral spectrum of photons generated through a Holographic Spectrograph and a Spiral Phase Plate, and subsequently verified with a multi-channel spectrometer and a diffraction grating in this experiment.

This note provides an exploration of the compactification methods for moduli spaces,
specifically algebraic and geometric, and their interconnections. We then
examine various examples to illustrate the contrast and commonality in these
different compactification approaches.

A mathematical model called a stochastic model is used to account for the random fluctuations in a two species ecosystem that's been studied over an extended period. This model considers external factors influencing the environment on both short and long-term bases. A significant finding from the study is that when one species suddenly takes over another, a specific pattern emerges in the ecosystem's noise - a 1/f pattern appears in the spectrum of short-term fluctuations. This is connected to a specific change in the system's capacity to sustain itself. Additionally, the researchers discovered that another indicator can effectively predict a significant shift in the population of species - the amplitude of low-frequency fluctuations. This amplitude fluctuation increases when the ecosystem is close to a critical transition point. This finding holds true when the environment experiences random variations on both short and long-term bases.

When comparing how much light galaxies emit to how fast they are forming new stars, we observe the same trend across most galaxies regardless of their mass. However, this equivalence breaks down above certain mass limits that vary depending on wavelength. Previous studies suggest a possible cause for this discrepancy could be large bulges found in many massive elliptical galaxies. In order to clarify the role bulges play in this phenomenon, a systematic analysis was conducted focusing on separate samples containing just either large bulges or small ones. This was done for various galaxies forming stars across the spectrum, both inside and outside of clusters, across the local universe. The findings indicate that in every instance, the presence of large bulges in these galaxies were associated with lower star formation rates, thus contributing to the observed decline in galaxy star formation rates at high masses when viewed through the lens of the UV to mid-IR spectrum.

This study focuses on sentiment assessment using C-LSA, a novel bilingual sentiment assessment dataset consisting of 84,000 Arabic and 36,000 English tweets with five sentiment labels.

We examine the impact of data efficiency and multi-task learning on class-level sentiment prediction, exploring various task configurations and training strategies including single-task and multi-way and few-shot learning.

Our experiments utilize the C-LSA dataset to validate the effectiveness of multi-task training and provide insight into the sentiment assessment process across languages.

This study examines how effectively two self-regulating practices can reduce perceived barriers in navigating online information. We gathered nearly 10,000 articles on a popular information portal and randomly showed participants pairs of them separated by various barriers. Approximately 1,000 participants indicated how many barriers they believed could be overcome using these practices. Our findings revealed that both practices were capable of reducing up to two effective barriers when exploring online information. Additionally, participants' problem-solving abilities improved after dealing with two barriers, as shown by their capacity to solve additional problems. Furthermore, participants' motivation to keep searching was heightened after applying these practices and found to be capable of reducing cognitive load, as well as being correlated with these practices' impact on mental processing. These results are corroborated by additional analytical findings.

Freiman's 3k-4 theorem generally posits that, for a prime number 'p', the number of sums of two elements from a subset A of the set of integers between 0 and p-1, will not equal or exceed $2p$, with the subset 'A' being of size 'k', and 'k' being both larger than or equal to $1000$ and have a ratio of elements 'A' to the set being less than or equal to $0.999\sqrt{\log\log k}/\log k$. 

We're showing a larger potential for 'p', and a greater minimum ratio of elements in the subset 'A', and the ratio includes an extra term of $1/\log\log\log\log k$.

We analyze the set of paths of fractional Brownian motion with an exponential growth rate, denoted as $\mathcal{C}_e^{fbm}$, and find the subset of paths that stay below a parabolic growth rate defined by $e^{(\frac{1}{2}+o(1))t}$ for a large fraction of time, denoted as $\mathcal{C}_{\le e^{1/2}}$. Our results indicate that $\mathcal{C}_e^{fbm}$ has a positive Lebesgue measure and an open subset in function space, as does the subset $\mathcal{C}_{\le e^{1/2}}$. These findings imply corresponding results for the set of paths of standard fractional Brownian motion under both polynomial and exponential scaling, revealing similar subsets with positive Lebesgue measure and open interiors.

This study reevaluates Dirac's variational principle, refining it to accommodate non-Hermitian operators and non-orthogonal trial functions. Leveraging this generalized form, we apply Dirac's variational method to estimate the H\'enon-Heiles system's H-atom ground state energy, demonstrating its effectiveness even for chaotic systems. Our results demonstrate close agreement with prior studies, particularly with those employing the Monte Carlo diffusion method. Furthermore, we extend the H\'enon-Heiles Hamiltonian using Dirac's variational principle to both periodic and chaotic regimes, consistently obtaining precise energy estimates in all phases. Our findings indicate that H-atom ground state energy remains stable across all H\'enon-Heiles Hamiltonian behavior, periodic, quasi-turbulent, or chaotic.

X-ray images of COVID-19 patients can be categorized into three groups based on severity: mild, moderate/severe, and ICU. Although the terms mild and moderate/severe are already defined in the dataset, the term ICU is absent in the original paper's section titles and should be replaced with its corresponding description. The authors have provided a detailed explanation of how to distinguish between these three categories, focusing on signs of severity such as oxygen saturation levels, respiratory distress, and visible lung abnormalities, which can be used to predict whether a patient will require admission to an intensive care unit.

This research paper establishes two key properties of simplicial groups in relation to simplicial bundles. Firstly, it proves that the total simplicial group to an assumed simplicial bundle is itself a simplicial group. Secondly, it demonstrates that a certain cross-section of this simplicial group contains a assumed simplicial group, providing a relational connection to the base space of the bundle. These findings are then applied to explore the characteristics of simplicial coverings and lifting functions. The proof of these claims builds upon a specific morphism construction, adapting an earlier proposal to examine simplicial bundles. This construction is also used to prove a corresponding theorem about the cross-section morphism in simplicial coverings. Additionally, it offers a proof of a specific feature of the long exact sequence in homotopy theory, relating to the first homotopy group.

A significant issue in Visual Relationship Detection (VRD) is the problem of false positives, where the model identifies non-existent relationships as real. This problem is compounded by data sparsity, particularly for rare categories and configurations. We discovered that a model with strong visual-language matching capabilities, Fine-grained Spatial Attention (FSA), can accurately identify occurrences of objects and their semantic locations, enabling it to filter out unrelated semantic pairs. We developed the Conquering Erroneous Positives (CEP) strategy, which leverages the FSA model's ability to filter out irrelevant pairs, thereby addressing the challenge of false positives. The Conquering Erroneous Positives (CEP) module is conqurred by replacing the conventional contrastive loss, which encourages matching, with a filtering loss, which seeks to conquer the False Positives (FPs). Conqurring the False Positives (CEP) module conqures the CEP challenge, thereby contributing to the improvement of the Visual Relationship Detection (VRD) model's performance. Conqurring the CEP challenge is a crucial step in the conquest of the Visual Relationship Detection (VRD) task.

A state-of-the-art activity recognition method based on deep learning requires a significant amount of training data and well-lit conditions.  To address this challenge, a new framework called Delta Sampling R-BERT has been proposed. This framework utilizes two primary techniques: a data-restricted sampling method that utilizes the central portion of mini-batches to represent the total dataset, thereby reducing the requirement for a significant amount of training data, and a low-light data enhancement method called Sigmoid-based Phase Adjustment (SPA) that adjusts the brightness of video activity sequences to maintain consistency across activities that occur in low-light conditions. These two techniques work together to enable a activity recognition model to be trained on a single-camera system with a large data set. Experimental results indicate that the proposed Delta Sampling R-BERT framework outperforms other methods in terms of accuracy, achieving a 97% accuracy rate on the KTH dataset.

A novel high-performance FPGA architecture called Data Addressable Concurrent
Processors (DACP) has been developed and demonstrated for AI/inference
applications with dense matrix multiplications as the primary operation. By
shifting the address generation and data movement responsibilities to processing
elements, the DACP architecture optimizes FPGA resource utilization and power
consumption, leaving more on-chip resources for actual computations. The DACP
concurrent processing element utilizes a modified datapath-based processing
element, integrating ALU and multiplexers to achieve efficient matrix
multiplications. A 2D DACP array with an SCM interface and router has been
designed, optimizing the firmware for Area Efficiency using the Yosys tool. The
128x128 DACP2 GFPGA prototype, synthesized on a Xilinx Virtex UltraScale+
platform, exhibits a 4.3 times area efficiency improvement and 2.3 times
performance gain when compared to existing FPGA accelerators.

We've discovered a high-redred galaxy at the perimeter of the Coma cluster, situated in a dense environment, where the host lies within 0.25 effective radii. This galaxy exhibits a remarkable disparity in color, with a delta U-V of 0.4 across its central regions and outer parts, indicating an asymmetry in the bulge-to-disk ratio. A thorough analysis using integral field spectroscopy indicates a host galaxy dominated by a star-forming, lopsided disk, with significant UV emission in the outer regions. In contrast, the central regions exhibit quiescence, lacking star creation, and contain a smaller fraction of a metal-rich population. These regions also exhibit an asymmetry in $\Delta V_{\rm rot}$ of 20 km/s, which may be attributed to a dense, sub-kiloparsec scale object. A high rate of star creation was observed at z=2.91 $\pm$ 0.05, primarily occurring within the galaxy's northern regions where the bulge-to-disk ratio is higher, and the metal content is lower, similar to the region with higher rotation rates. This suggests a possible relationship between the development of bulges and star creation in this galaxy, potentially due to the galaxy's asymmetry, as it is situated in the outer regions of the galaxy, and its orientation, as it is not at the center of the galaxy, is not influencing the observed activity.

We employ both existing and newly acquired flavour global data to examine the hypothesis of Structure Zero – the notion that flavour arises when particle structures transition from point-like to composite forms. A statistical assessment of Structure Zero's claim uses a Markov Chain Monte Carlo method to determine the probability of the current structural state given the global data. Our analysis reveals that, as point-like and composite structures compete for description of fundamental particles, flavour quarks demonstrate an evident shift towards composite descriptions, suggesting that quarks may not be fundamental, but rather composed of as yet unidentified constituents.

This paper aims to provide solutions for the steady Navier-Stokes equation coupled with the Poiseuille equation, incorporating a periodic, compactly supported cubic term. We have earlier obtained the primary result for this system in two-dimensional space and now extend that finding to any dimension greater than or equal to three. This advancement gives the first positive confirmation of a predicted "bubbling" phenomenon for the standalone cubic equation in dimensions greater than or equal to three.

Proprietary tools for source code analysis are often employed to identify and rectify bugs before the code is deployed, yet research platforms are typically utilized for studying code changes' effects. This paper presents an alternative approach to analyzing code revisions, utilizing neural models to predict revision outcomes based on static evaluation. Our experimental results show that the model can generate revised code updates that are of comparable quality to human-made fixes, but with roughly ten times less effort. This, in turn, shows the potential of the predictive approach and paves the way for integrating it into automated code repair systems.

A solar neutron decomposition event took place on November 7, 2004, with observations of solar neutrons by the CRRES satellite and nuclear activation of the GOES-15 geosynchronous geoscope between 10:00 and 11:00 UT. This study utilized the CRRES data to calculate the flux of solar neutrons and identified a significant decrease in neutron flux, or decomposition, for the first time. Furthermore, an estimate of the decomposition of solar protons was made based on GOES-15 data, or it could not be determined due to insufficient detection of gamma rays. A comparison of electron spectra from before and after the decomposition, or between the events on GOES-15 and CRRES, was also performed.

In this study, we examined the dispersion relations for linearized relativistic fluid dynamics, taking into account rotation and acceleration effects. Our analysis builds upon previous work by Fock and utilizes both a kinetic theory approach through the relaxation time approximation of Boltzmann's equation and a purely hydrodynamic analysis. Our results demonstrate the emergence of primary and secondary Galilean invariance in a linearized context and reveal that acceleration effects can lead to new forms of primary and secondary invariance. We found that in a non-relativistic context, secondaries invariance is restored when using a first-order fluid dynamics model.

Our proposed anomaly identification method, InQMAD, takes a incremental approach using quantum measurement embedding. By converting measurement outcomes into high-dimensional vectors that capture the system's state, InQMAX detects changes through an outlier score based on support vector machines. As more data is added, the model retrained from scratch, ensuring precise anomaly detection with a minimal impact of concept drift on performance. Furthermore, the parallel nature of quantum measurement and automated embedding generation allows for rapid processing and real-world application with a built-in evaluation metric for detection speed.

A pressing concern in the age of end-to-end encrypted messaging is the possibility of a government entity forcing users to provide their passwords or backdoors being installed in apps to facilitate decryption by the state. We investigate the extent to which the state can compel the coercion of decryption, assuming a scenario in which the message recipient is fully aware of the state's involvement. A mathematical model is developed under these assumptions. The model's implications are explored in the context of several popular encrypted messaging platforms, including WhatsApp, Telegram, Signal, and iMessage.

We present a novel universal framework to simulate the measurement-device-independent quantum key distribution (MDI-QKD) process, which is crucial for securing quantum communication networks. This framework is built on Python and utilizes quPy, an open-source quantum programming tool. It enables users to freely design and build custom quantum circuits for MDI-QKD, without needing to specify the underlying physical implementation. As a result, this framework facilitates efficient exploration and optimization of different MDI-QKD circuit designs to enhance their performance. We illustrate the framework's potential by developing two leading MDI-QKD designs and by introducing an optimized design that shows improved performance with an enhanced gain-fluctuation variance and a 10% increase in the final key rate. This framework is also ideal for integrating and visualizing data graphs through the use of GnuPlot, thereby enabling more effective analysis and interpretation of results.

Approximate weighted circuit satisfiability, which is a specific case of the maximum clique problem, serves as a fundamental and extensively researched parameter in optimization. This paper introduces a novel approximate weighted circuit satisfiability algorithm, which, for problems with a limited number of variables per clause, guarantees an outcome close to the optimal solution. This algorithm employs a PTAS approach, which, despite being computationally expensive, can be conceptually related to a basic approximation technique for the maximum clique problem. In contrast, existing methods for circuit satisfiability often lack approximations due to their inherent complexity. This problem, which is NP-hard even when considering limited complexity classes, hinders the development of efficient solutions in scenarios involving large-scale problems, such as training neural networks. This research proposes a PTAS for circuit satisfiability problems involving a finite number of clauses, provided the clauses are assigned a specific type of weight. This algorithm, although not applicable to all circuit satisfiability problems, serves as a significant step towards developing efficient solutions for problems with sparse clauses.

This study presents a novel, high-order numerical solution for a specific Fokker-Planck equation, often used in average field games to model interactions within large populations. The high-order Lagrange-Galerkin method is employed, and the implementation over B-spline meshes is designed to be robust against time-step changes. This approach ensures a second-order accuracy in both time and spatial calculations, resulting in a computationally efficient algorithm suitable for solving complex, real-world average field games problems.

Artificial Intelligence, specifically Deep Neural Networks (DNNs), has transformed complex tasks that were previously intractable. Nonetheless, the lack of understanding humans have of how DNNs reach conclusions has been a significant barrier to their widespread adoption in fields where human-DNN collaboration is essential. This research aims to bridge this gap by using visual representations to make the DNNs' decision-making processes more accessible to humans. Furthermore, we assessed the level of comprehension that both humans and a DNN explanation framework (Counterfactual Intervenability Analysis, CIA) have of various visualizations, such as Saliency Maps, Deep LIFT, Counterfactual Explanations, and Layer-wise Relevance Propagation. Our findings revealed that while the CIA framework's visualizations made the most sense, they also had room for improvement when it came to providing accurate justifications. Additionally, the study established a unified evaluation method for explanation frameworks, which could serve as a benchmark for future research.

Astronomers have observed that up to 30% of young planetary embryos approaching the surface of forming planets are spinning too fast for a calm state, known as the oligo-accretion model of planetary growth to account for. This phenomenon occurs especially often around 10 AU from their star, and even more so in systems with numerous small bodies. To address this issue, we conducted computer simulations of the planet formation process under these high-spin conditions using the Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics method. These simulations revealed a completely unanticipated solution: a planet can transfer angular momentum to nearby debris through a process called "spinning-up the surface," thereby slowing down and allowing it to accrete material for further growth. This discovery reveals that planets can grow despite receiving material that is spinning too fast for them to handle and still be consistent with observations of forming planetary systems.

The surge in deep-fake videos has caused significant worries about the reliability of compromised information, with research focusing on employing multiple modalities to reduce this risk.

However, because the models used in these studies are trained before the release, they eventually get vulnerable to tailored attacks aimed at faking news.

In this research, a new approach called Meta Neural Process Networks (Meta-NPN) for identifying false news across multiple modalities is proposed, where the deployment of this approach requires a single model component, also known as the Neural Progressive Approximation (NPN).

Essentially, NPN infers the implicit elements of model parameters that have been corrupted, by analyzing multiple modalities of data. This allows it to identify false news, even with a single modality.

By serving as a meta-model atop an existing model, it transforms this into a continuous meta-learning task. We evaluate Meta-NPN on multiple modalities of emergent false news, using extensive experiments and a comparative analysis to demonstrate the superiority of this research in identifying false news compared to current state-of-the-art methods.

This study delves into the complex dynamics of a periodic transport equation, 
which arises in the analysis of fluid velocity patterns in non-degenerating degenerate parabolic equations. 
We have exactly solved this problem and provide a general solution in the case of a periodic transport. 
Our findings reveal three key anomalies - some of which have not been previously known - about the 
periodic conveyance equation: 
(1) the solution may exhibit an unexpected increase in the number of non-zero values as time progresses; 
(2) the solution's behavior near the boundary may be influenced by initial conditions from outside the domain; 
and (3) the solution's structure may become highly intricate, with emerging intricate patterns of zero values. 
These findings have significant implications for understanding the broader class of transport equations.

In systems like caching and information updating, there's often a need to reload content or reload updated versions of that content. A new instance is considered as generation 1, and replacing an existing instance with a new one marks the start of a higher generation. The generation period is defined as the time it takes for an instance to be replaced by another instance of the same generation. Understanding the distribution of generation periods is crucial for analyzing content and information system designs. This paper focuses on calculating the distribution of these periods in a specific type of queueing system and provides examples in areas such as caching and information updating where this concept is applied. Additionally, it examines the case of multiple servers in a parallel setup.

A new class of algebraic structures called set-theoretic genre solutions of the Yang-Baxter equation is introduced, which is a variation of set-theoretic race solutions. It is then demonstrated that when a set-theoretic genre solution exists on a given set, it can give rise to a quasi-bialgebra by applying mathematical constructions to the Hopf algebra derived from the free associative algebra generated by that set.

A novel class of codes known as Golay complementary sets (GCS) of N-tuples will be discussed, comprising N-dimensional vectors of complex numbers or binary numbers. If the elements of the GCS are binary numbers, we refer to them as binary Golay complementary sets (BGCS). Researchers have long been interested in finding efficient methods for creating GCS or BGCS with a variety of dimensions N. Some of these methods have resulted in creation formulas that only allow N to take on specific values, while a method discovered by Amram and Shokrollahi in 1999 enabled N to any desired number of dimensions, though it limited the elements of the generated tuples to Gaussian integers. A method will be demonstrated for creating new sets of GCS with a large cross set of T-tuples, where each tuple has a distinct dimension N. If the elements of the BGCS are binary numbers, a corresponding method for creating large cross sets of T-tuples with dimensions N will be shown. An application discovered in showing the application of the proposed method, it enables the creation of a binary multi-phase complementary set (BCPCS) of N-tuples with a large cross set of T-tuples. An application discovered in showing the application of the proposed method, it enables N to any desired positive even integer, resulting in a new lower bound of the binary Hadamard conjecture. An application discovered in showing the application of the proposed method, it enables N to any desired positive even

In this work, measurements of tunneling between a tungsten atomic probe and a tungsten atom adsorbed on silicon are conducted to examine the interplay of atomic scale electronic correlations between two adjacent atoms in materials that possess two-valley wave functions. The study reveals a pronounced resonance in spin-polarized current as the distance between the probe and target atoms increases, occurring beyond the localized $s$-orbital regime and occurring at the point of maximal overlap between their two-valley wave functions. The threshold for coupling and the observed resonance are used to calibrate the energy scale of the hybridized orbitals in tungsten.

Complex systems failing due to cascades are highly nonlinear and dynamic, with their internal structure often being unknown. Neighboring elements within these systems can exert a significant influence on the dynamics of the system, with the connectivity between them evolving over time. To address this complexity, a graph neural network framework has been developed that utilizes a message-passing mechanism to capture both the spatial and temporal aspects of dynamic systems. Using this model, researchers were able to accurately predict how systems such as power grids behave during dynamic events. Furthermore, they investigated multiple theories of system failures, including the Rostoff model, by simulating events and observing their effects. This led to an improved understanding of external factors that contribute to system failures, as well as a more robust defense against cyber attacks on the internet. To avoid the need for costly interventions, researchers also studied the underlying causes of misinformation on social media, with promising results.

This study follows up on a recent finding by the author, which established a connection between the homotopy groups of a specific algebraic structure and the division cases within a specific algebraic theory, and further developed the connection to a related algebraic theory, homotopical matroidology. The study's main achievement is to expand the set of division cases considered, thereby providing more comprehensive information about the homotopy groups.

Certain neural network components can lead to unwanted cognitive behavioral changes,
known as hallucinations. This issue poses a significant challenge in clinical brain lesion
segmentation, where abnormalities in patient behavior can complicate the task. To tackle
this problem, we developed a cerebral lesion generation network, called P-ALL, built on
the principle of Progressive Adversarial Variational Auto-Encoders. P-ALL incorporates
gradual complexity increases in its encoding process, allowing it to efficiently capture
hallucinations and improve clinical brain lesion generation accuracy. To counter the
overgeneration of lesions, we introduced a suppression mechanism, effectively preventing
uncontrolled hallucinations in patient behavior and enhancing clinical brain lesion
performance. The core idea of progressive learning was also applied to the P-ALL network,
resulting in better generalization and control over the distribution of hallucinations and
clinical brain lesions. The experiment confirmed that the Adversarial Loss and Suppression
Mechanism, in conjunction with the progressive encoding of pall, can efficiently model
both types of neural network components, leading to superior clinical brain lesion
segmentation performance.

The striking phenomenon of quantum nonlocality, which outperforms classical influences in remote effect manipulation, can arise not only in quantum superpositions but also in mixed states through entanglement. However, practical applications are hindered by the fragility of such states, extremely pure, and homogeneous requirements. In this research, we introduce an innovative nonlocality demonstration, robust against noise, involving probabilistic protocols using mixed states, and can be achieved with the minimal degree of entanglement in a mixed-state framework, and with unity in three-qubit systems. This finding provides an interesting connection between quantum nonlocality and entanglement, and we identify specific combinations of local densities in homogeneous or heterogeneous systems that can produce nonlocal behavior, thus proving the potential of such configurations.

The analysis of massive datasets in the fifth data release of the Sloan Digital Sky Survey demands the coordination of numerous distributed robots known as astrobots. To accomplish this, a secure coordination mechanism called Totally Secure Coordination (TSC) has been implemented on the SDSS-V astrobots. In this mechanism, the astrobots' interactions are modeled using a Totally Observational Petri Net (TOPN), which is then used to verify the system's compliance with desired specifications through model checking techniques in the 2TBFBPA language. A key aspect of TSC is that the verification processes remain confidential from external observation, a property that was experimentally validated using the astrobots' coordinates system as a modeling framework for the investigation.

GP 2 is a high-level language built on top of Gandalf 2, leveraging an existing compiler. It utilizes Gandalf 2's optimizer and instruction set architecture to create efficient and compact code. GP 2 allows language designers to define grammar rules, operator precedence, and semantics, resulting in a compact program size and efficient execution. GP 2 also includes a debugger that uses Gandalf 2's debugger, making it easy to identify and fix bugs.

A prominent characteristic of deep learning models, known as feature extractors or feature encoders, has fueled their widespread adoption. However, developing a universally applicable feature extractor remains a significant challenge due to the lack of a standard architecture. In contrast to traditional methods that rely on transfer learning and fine-tuning, our proposed comparative learning approach aims to create a single, unified structure for a specific application. By combining contrastive and self-supervised comparative learning, we can design one unified architecture that effectively extracts high-quality features. Our approach not outperforms a range of comparable methods but also provides a framework for future research in machine learning. Notably, our proposed unified structure achieves superior performance in the context of classification and regression tasks.

In this investigation, we demonstrate a novel pattern in quotient diagrams of specific groups where, for a twisted wreath group G = AwrB with identical base groups (A=B), each block in a pair of isomorphic components reveals an isomorphic copy of a smaller diagram. This characteristic allows us to derive multiple instances of star normal quotient diagrams of twisted wreath groups.

Working with nominal data in statistical and machine learning fields is
challenging, especially when dealing with large and complex datasets. High-
dimensional nominal data can be group sparsely structured, which presents both
a challenge and a valuable opportunity for more efficient and interpretable
modeling. We have tackled this issue by integrating the concept of subgradients
with the R-package 'GroupLasso', allowing for optimization of nominal regression
models with hidden and interpretable structures. Our package, nlmer, employs a
smart initial parameter estimation technique to optimize model performance,
resulting in enhanced accuracy, reduced complexity, improved interpretability,
and better overall model fit compared to previous methods.

Large, language-based models have recently made significant progress in various linguistic tasks due to models like BERT and GPT-2. Despite this progress, there's a lack of standardization in how models are set up and configured, which poses challenges for managing models across enterprises. To address this issue, we present a framework called ABILITY, a manageable and modular system for configuring and managing knowledge enhancements in models through third-party sources. Built on top of the Django web application framework, ABILITY provides a consistent API for models to access a wide range of external information, from factual knowledge to models of real-world processes and human expertise. We demonstrate the benefits of ABILITY in areas such as medical diagnosis, business strategy, general reasoning and more, and our source code is publicly available at https://github.com/ability-django/ability-django.

The study examines a specific type of nonlocal dispersion model, specifically one that uses power laws to describe influence. The research reveals that under certain conditions, this model converges to a first-order hyperbolic conservation law. Additionally, it shows that it also matches the limits of the Pham-Carrion nonlocal diffusion model. Furthermore, the study provides proof that the numerical solutions of the initial model converge to those of the hyperbolic and diffusion limits with a rate of $O(\tau)$, where $\tau$ denotes the characteristic length scale of nonlocal interaction.

Traditional panoramic stitching techniques are limited to a single exposure around a subject, unable to capture scenes obstructed by a subject from multiple angles. This work introduces a novel approach to stitching images based on the principle of gravity, which has been shown to be a reliable principle consistently observable in nature. We formulate a minimal action model grounded in this principle, assuming that objects tend to align with the direction of gravity. This approach allows us to derive a simple, energy-based model of a single exposure around a subject, as well as a more complex model for multiple exposures. These models are capable of accurately representing the dynamics of a single or multiple exposures around a subject. We then develop a basic algorithm to stitch images based on these models. Experimental results demonstrate that this approach can accurately recover the scene from data.
This paper delves into the cancellation of local Eisenseries at $p$ in detail, with a specific focus on how the Zeilberger algorithm can be employed to achieve this.

This paper presents a novel biophysical computational model for Parkinson's disease, tailored to marmoset moneys. Barring a cure, Parkinson's disease management relies on tailored medication and surgical procedures, supplemented by physical and cognitive therapy to maintain mobility and balance. We developed a unique, biophysically-based computational model, utilizing marmoset data, to simulate the dopaminergic system's decline, motor control system's Parkinson's-related impairments, and the effects of standard treatments. This model integrates marmoset-specific anatomical and physiological data with a open-source, whole-muscle activation model, enabling more accurate simulation of atrophy's progression, falls, and balance disruptions. Furthermore, the model incorporates therapy, surgical, and pharmacological interventions to enhance motor function.

When converting high-precision line layers into scalable vector graphics, the number of lines often leads to rendering issues due to anti-aliasing challenges that basic algorithms fail to address effectively. To resolve this, we've developed a novel approach that utilizes anti-aliasing effects at line junctions to convey rich information through limited line width, allowing for smoother rendering results. By applying this concept, we were able to create an efficient anti-aliasing algorithm that processes path data at specific points and employs precise start and end point treatments along with dynamic line width adjustments. The results show a significant reduction in rendering errors and smearing artifacts under various test scenarios, with rendering performances also being 1.5 to 2 times faster than expected.

We report on a new set of 9 optically thin ultraluminous/ luminous infrared galaxies below 0.04 in redshift using the Seimei Telescope and the KOOLS-IFU. These 9 targets, located in the GOALS collection, are situated in major merger events and will be observed with the KOOLS-IFU for a total of 10.8 hours. Our observations are contributing to the broader Seimei Deep Field project. We conducted our analysis on the internal kinematics and gas outflows of these 9 galaxies, as well as their chemical compositions. We found evidence of high-velocity gas outflows in 3 of the 9 galaxies, as well as complex superposed gas components in 4 of the 9 galaxies. We also found multiple emission lines in 3 regions of the 9 galaxies, as well as rotating gas disks in 5 regions of the 9 galaxies. These observations are consistent with the highly dynamic and complex nature of these galaxy merger sites, as well as the potential for KOOLS-IFU to provide in-depth insights into galaxy mergers and starbursts.

The multivariate interpolation operator is traditionally studied using a cardinal operator, which however fails to satisfy the bounded derivative property, making it inflexible for functions with bounded derivatives. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a non-degenerate, transcendental interpolation operator based on the MinstRf transcendental radial basis function, which maintains the smoothness of the original function and provides a bounded derivative, thereby enabling accurate and reliable approximations. We also establish a convergence theorem for the interpolation process, which indicates that the interpolation error converges to zero at a rate of h^s, where s is the degree of the Rbf and h is the maximum distance between interpolation points.

Accurate navigation systems are crucial for both passengers and drivers, as they provide essential route guidance and estimated times of arrival. Adverse weather conditions can significantly delay or cancel travel plans, underscoring the need for effective weather forecasting. Advances in computer weather forecasting have made it possible to predict the type of weather with a high degree of accuracy. This study explores the development of a high-quality, multi-class dataset containing clear, rainy, snowy, and foggy images, along with a data processing technique to improve estimation times of arrival in various weather conditions. Our evaluations of convolutional neural network algorithms, including mass-produced models, have yielded a precise approach to weather classification that outperforms existing methods. Our method's error rate is 8.75% across four types of weather, compared to the average industry error rate of 17.5%.

To restore the speech quality of compromised audio recordings, we've developed a novel end-to-end model called the Dual-Path Convolution Recurrent Network (DPCRN). This network, which builds on the conventional Convolution Recurrent Network (CRN), incorporates an additional pathway to effectively capture both temporal and spectral patterns in the input audio. Experimental results show that the DPCRN significantly outperforms the baseline CRN model, achieving a 0.6 dB improvement in word error rate on the Librispeech dataset. Furthermore, we've discovered that a smaller DPCRN model matches the performance of a larger CRN model, suggesting potential applications on resource-constrained devices.

A quantum gravity theory called $f(R)$ gravity replaces general relativity's R term in the gravitational action, with specific models identified by their additional degrees of degree of freedom, denoted as 'm', with a value of m=0 for the standard R model. These models significantly impact the size of dark matter halo, particularly near the galaxy's center, by altering the rate of galaxy expansion and the mass of neutrinos that constitute a minor fraction of the halo's mass. We investigated how $f(R)$ gravity models and heavy neutrinos affect the turn-around radii of dark matter halos, discovering that models with higher values of 'm' produce smaller halos, an effect amplified when accounting for the presence of heavy neutrinos. Specifically, for an $m=10$ model, the turn-around radius of a galaxy formed under $f(R)$ gravity is about 15% smaller than that predicted by $\Lambda$CDM theory.

This study aims to develop single-column models (SCMs) using a multi-fluid framework for both horizontal and temperature velocities, with the potential to incorporate sub-grid variability in future atmospheric convection simulations. We first tested this framework by simulating the Rayleigh-B\'{e}nard convection, with results showing accurate reproduction of various characteristics when using a two-fluid model. However, to better assess the advantages and challenges of a two-fluid framework over its single-fluid counterpart, we conducted simulation experiments under various resolution settings and with different numbers of fluid elements. Findings indicated that, at higher resolutions, differences between the single and multi-fluid simulations became negligible. At lower resolutions, we identified notable discrepancies, with simulations using two or more fluid elements resulting in significantly different simulations when compared to their single-fluid counterparts.

A network of isolated nodes is analyzed, where the correlations between adjacent nodes are controlled by Jaynes-Cummings interactions, creating an system exhibiting Rabi oscillations.  An important finding arises when the coupling strength between nodes varies, showing that the dynamics of coupled systems leads to genuine entanglement between the qubits, even without direct interaction.  This entanglement exhibits notable non-monotonic behavior in relation to Rabi frequencies, creating opportunities for enhanced entanglement generation by adjusting the vacuum Rabi frequency.  Notable findings indicate optimal entanglement, measured by concurrence, reaches a peak value of one, corresponding to specific Rabi frequencies, particularly when ratios are an even integer and half-odd integer.  Research reveals that entanglement generation efficiency is significantly improved when nodes are linked by systems with varying Rabi frequencies, allowing for up to a two-fold increase in concurrence within the node network.

The CMS detector at the LHC has undergone significant upgrades to adapt to the much higher luminosity environments anticipated for Phase-2.  However, certain upgraded detector components are not exposed to the highest central regions where phantom data may interfere with performance.  As such, a dedicated layer of the original pixel detector was retained and designed to be aligned both longitudinally and radially, despite being exposed to intense radiation.  This untouched layer, known as the pilot layer, is primarily focused on identifying muons and heavy ions.  With three times as many readout chips, the pilot layer collects nearly half of the total detection area.  This layer sits just before the outer edge of the endcaps, making it ideal for studying hadron jets and quark jets.  This paper examines the performance of the pilot layer in reconstructing jet particles one year after it was installed, using data from proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV and an integrated luminosity of 35.6 inverse femtobarns.  The results when comparing the reconstruction of jets that originate from heavy ions show a good match with expectations, whereas the examinations of standard model processes indicate minor but statistically notable discrepancies, particularly at higher signal-to-background signals.  As for reconstructing the momentum of reconstructed particles, the responses are generally consistent with what is expected within 5-10 percent statistical uncertainty, although there are some deviations of less than two standard deviations in certain high

A comprehensive examination of the Kall\'en-Lehmann spectral density for the scalar glueball spectrum in SU(2) QCD was performed, utilizing a rigorous, first-principles approach. Key features of the spectral density were analyzed, and the masses of the lowest lying glueball states were precisely determined to be $2.195(7)$ GeV for $0^{++}$, $3.373(15)$ GeV for $2^{++}$, and $4.504(24)$ GeV for $0^{-+}$, representing the most accurate and precise estimates to date, while also offering in-depth insights into previously estimated values.

Social media monitoring through sentiment analysis enables the assessment of public opinion. Leveraging Twitter's vast user base, this analysis can be highly effective. Utilizing text from Twitter posts, sentiment evaluation enables the prediction of public sentiment based on keywords that trigger emotions. To predict sentiment evaluation scores, a 3-tiered Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network is employed. This network is composed of Chinese Character Embedding, Sentiment Evaluation Word Embedding, and 2-tier LSTM components. The character embedding generates character vectors, while the word embedding vectors are produced by processing each post character by character. Similarly, the sentiment evaluation words are vectorized. Each vector is then fed into the 2-tier LSTM, which outputs the sentiment evaluation score. To optimize training, a sentiment evaluation dataset is compiled by having humans rate the sentiment of online comments on a scale of 1 to 5. The model is then trained and its performance is assessed through the sentiment evaluation dataset.

A linear response framework, specifically the membrane paradigm, has been applied to derive a simplified model of black holes, resulting in 'shadow' quantities that correspond to observable phenomena from distant observers. In a recent study, the authors employed the non-linear Maxwell theory to investigate the dynamic properties of a charged black hole within a non-singular, asymptotically AdS spacetime, utilizing the membrane paradigm. The results of the investigation revealed the speed of sound varies in response to the linearity of the Maxwell theory, while the viscosity ratio displays significant variation depending on the charge of the black hole, with infinite values being produced by both Einstein-Maxwell-CCGK and a linearized Maxwell-CCGK models.

A new method is proposed to quantify entanglement and quantum-classical transition in quantum tomograms, which are experimental reconstructions of quantum states. This approach is based on the ability of quantum tomograms to entangle and differentiate between entangled and classical mixed states. A specific example, involving a Bell-diagonal state and local operations applied to an EPR state, is analyzed to illustrate these concepts.

The advent of powerful, pre-trained language models has significantly
streamlined the task of generating dialogue, but there's still a lack of
well-engineered systems that incorporate these models to build comprehensive
conversation applications. We've constructed a conversation platform,
'ConvAI-Roles', where a role is specified in detail, providing the
builder of the system with a detailed blueprint to follow. Our role definition
includes a purposeful component, which encompasses a dialogue model, background
knowledge, and a conversation strategy. We've also provided a comprehensive
set of role-related components, including semantic understanding, text management,
and data modeling. Our system has demonstrated its effectiveness in building
various types of conversations, including those centered around a particular
subject, and we've also explored the implications of different design choices
on the conversation's quality. Our work has led to the creation of three
distinctively defined roles, as well as a large-scale dataset to evaluate the
impact of the conversation strategy. Our research indicates that ConvAI-Roles
can achieve human-comparable performance, but still leaves room for improvement.
Our work has also made all systems and data accessible to the research
community.

Decision-making in agriculture can be tackled more robustly using a modified form of the 0/1 Knapsack Problem, which accounts for the adverse effects of unselected items. This variation is solved using a change to the objective function and a well-established solution method. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated in strawberry pest control, where the choice between chemical pesticides and biological controls is made to maximize crop yield. The problem is formulated specifically for this application and the results are analyzed through a case study.

Forecasting where a traveler is headed within a 360-degree video is a crucial step in creating an engaging and efficient immersive video experience. A common approach to evaluating forecasting accuracy involves assessing the overlap between 360-degree spheres, yet this method can be misleading as even a minimal overlap may signify an inaccurate forecast, and the method falls short as it considers only the final video frame's viewpoint, ignoring human visual tendencies that always focus on the best image quality near the center of the field. To address these limitations, we propose a novel error measurement approach that accurately evaluates forecasting captions and leverages viewer travel patterns to learn traveler preferences for end-captsions. Additionally, we present a more realistic model that models the probability of gaze points falling within a specific range, instead of a single point.

A tensor network construction called LEAN-NPE has been developed to represent a wide range of thermal states in lattice models, suitable for computing physical properties in different dimensions. By leveraging local approximations through a specific type of tensor decomposition, this model can accurately describe thermal expectation values on the same lattice structure, has a manageable bond dimension that scales linearly with $\beta/J$, and exhibits favorable scaling for dynamic processes in one-dimensional systems. Furthermore, the framework provides an efficient derivation of the Gibbs reduction for certain models and suggests generalizing results based on their thermodynamic behavior.

Our research decouples complex effective theories from their underlying high-energy theories by introducing two restricted efficacy operations that limit what an agent can achieve. The first restriction can be decoupled by decoupling mappings -- able to preserve the ability to execute a restricted task within an alternative system. The first restriction comprises a task that a given agent can successfully complete. A decoupling mapping can be found if and only if there exists a sequence of scale-oriented approximations of the task. These approximations represent a series of simpler tasks that are easier to decide and solve, and can be progressively replaced by entities from an alternative system. Notably, scale-oriented approximations involve decoupling through decision and solving replacements. Oracles and agents are then constructed to execute the sequence of simpler tasks. A decision tree and decoupling operator can be developed from the answers to queries about the alternative system. A key feature of scale-oriented approximations is that they are decided and solved by the decision tree and agent. If a decision tree and agent can be decoupled, then an approximation is decision and solving approximated. A decision and solving approximation is essentially an exact match. If only decision and solving approximations are possible, then any entity from the alternative system that can execute a complex task must exist in the system of the original agent.
