The concept of absorbing wave energy efficiently in the middle of a two-dimensional system is explored, where the outer boundary consists of an insulating barrier. A group of internal points is identified that maximize the absorption of incoming waves by a specific type of scattering matrix. It's discovered that this maximum absorption increases significantly when the system enters a disordered state. The nature of the incoming waves leads to two distinct summaries of maximum absorption eigenchannels: one where the chaotic system results in absorbed power being related to conductance, and another where the quasi-periodic system relates it to the local conductance. These findings are theoretically derived using sum rules and supported by numerical simulations.

A novel class of 3D topological Anderson insulators arising from random binary imperfections in cubic lattices is analyzed. Using effective medium theory, a simplified model describing these systems with high accuracy is created. The model's 3D topological characteristics are deduced from the quasi-momentum characteristics of the corresponding disordered tight-binding model in 3D space. The findings indicate that a wide range of random imperfections can generate 3D topological Anderson conductors in the negative energy bands of the clean cubic system. The model also allows for an exact calculation of the 3D Chern number, revealing that it increases as the ratio of the disorder strength to the atomic tunneling amplitude in the cubic lattice does.

This study focuses on specific group theory concepts, including $TR$-isomorphisms between $p$-groups and $q$-groups, as well as truncated groups in relation to $p$-groups and solvable groups. We demonstrate that any two $TR$-isomorphic $p$-groups and $q$-groups cannot be of comparable prime size, while proving that groups with the same $TR$-isomorphism status as solvable groups of a given prime order can already be found among truncated solvable groups of the same prime length. These concepts and findings are supported by relevant definitions and relevant theorems.

A novel mechanism for generating the observed Higgs boson at the ~125 GeV mass level is presented, involving radiative symmetry breaking with non-zero Higgs masses and a secondary, unobserved state for the lightest Higgs boson, involving a MSSM parameter space with intricate interconnections, possibly extending the Standard Model's Hadron Dark Matter sector into its own, self-contained 'hadaton' sector.

Researchers have traditionally used network autoregressive (NAR) models with an assumption of linearity, which may have limited their applicability. To address this limitation, we developed a new, non-linear generalization of the NAR framework that accounts for network structures. We created two innovative likelihood-based likelihood ratio (LR) tests to evaluate the linearity assumption in this new framework. These tests consider different levels of complexity in the non-linear alternative framework and an important interaction between the network and the response variable. A simulation study was conducted to assess the performance of the LR tests and discovered that increasing levels of non-linearity and various types of networks affect test performance. Additionally, we applied our methodology to a dataset of US house prices, demonstrating the benefits of using the non-linear framework. Our results suggest that at higher price levels, non-linearities and an interaction between network and price arise, resulting in more accurate price predictions.

This study focuses on issue framework in the context of deep declarative networks, specifically examining its applications in medical image classification and medical image segmentation.  
An analysis of the issue in declarative networks is conducted, followed by an investigation into potential solutions.  Two case studies are presented to validate the issues identified in declarative networks and the subsequent issues arising from using one-shot encoders and inverse functions for segmentation tasks.  
It is hypothesized that the observed performance decline in medical image segmentation results from the negative impact of one-shot encoders on the increase of semantic entropy in latent variables.  
To address these issues, a novel approach is introduced that employs distinct declarative networks with separate sets of declarative variables to facilitate med image classification and segmentation.  
The proposed method demonstrated superior performance when compared to the current state-of-the-art techniques in medical image classification and outscored the existing approaches in medical image segmentation when evaluated on two benchmark datasets.

A biological entity known as a cell is comprised of many interrelated components that are crucial in understanding cell behavior. This paper is looking for a structural understanding of these components in order to effectively create models that can capture cell dispersal, motility and the relocation of proteins on a cell's lipid membrane. This process is also influenced by the dynamic nature of the cell's outer surface. To this end, we are presenting a new model called an Hierarchical Stochastic PDE System (HSPS) that can create equations which are both manageable and provide a clear picture of cell functionality. This model is further applied to two well-known biological phenomena: the dispersion of a retinal cell and the relocation of proteins in a fruit fly's larval cell. Our work is also exploring a more abstract, mathematical description of cell operation. This is achieved by utilizing a multi-scale, stochastic framework (MSS) that can create a comprehensive model of cell functionality. This, in turn, is used to develop equations which can capture the cell's behavior. To this end, we are presenting a new theoretical framework that can provide a clear mathematical foundation for the HSPS model. This framework is further illustrated by two specific examples: the dispersion of a retinal cell and the relocation of proteins in a fruit fly's larval cell. Our work is also exploring the potential for this framework to be used in conjunction with the HSPS model to effectively address a broader range of cell-related issues.

The rapid adoption of cryptocurrencies, particularly Bitcoin, has also created opportunities for criminals to exploit them. Although researchers have studied methods to detect criminal activities in cryptocurrency networks, there's a lack of understanding of the complex mechanisms behind these networks that enable criminal actions. This study bridges this gap by providing a comprehensive analysis of criminal activities within cryptocurrency networks and their underlying complexity. To fulfill this analysis, a complex network is constructed from raw blockchain transaction data, which is then used to examine how transactions are connected over time to uncover the hidden complexity of these financial networks through measures like small-world properties and modular structures. Furthermore, the research develops a six-stage pathway system that categorizes the flow of funds during money laundering and investment activities and illustrates them with real-world examples. The findings of this study can be applied to design more effective defense mechanisms against cryptocurrency crimes by guiding the creation of targeted intervention strategies.

Quantum computing's transformative potential in complex computational areas is hindered by technical technical challenges, particularly the failure of quantum bits and cross-talk. We are proposing a novel, failure-tolerant quantum computing framework that focuses on two key areas: automatically creating robust quantum circuits for specific tasks and optimizing quantum hardware for task resilience. We have developed a cohesive framework consisting of this specialized hardware and software, which integrates a new form of reinforcement learning-powered C-coding and a targeted error-reduction technique. The result is an efficient system that produces highly reliable quantum circuits and improves their resilience by minimizing gate count. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this framework by automatically creating high-performance quantum circuits for central bank policy estimation, outperforming previous methods in both accuracy and resilience.

Precise sensing and navigation are crucial in modern navigation systems, particularly those based on inertial technology, which quickly accumulate errors. Two axes of such technologies, ring laser gyros, can deliver highly sensitive directionality data thanks to their unique dual-cavity structure that supports a particular quantum intensity fluctuation known as the hybrid shot noise. This study investigates the role of quantum shot noise in enhancing measurement sensitivity by examining the dynamics of a system of bose-einstein condensates coupled to the laser system. The ultimate capacity for sensitive measurements of system dynamics or external influences influencing its behavior is investigated. The study also explores the possibility of achieving quantum-enhanced sensitivity in this specific scenario and identifies the optimal method for extracting information to maximize the amount of obtainable directionality data.

The PHENIX Collaboration analyzed direct photon-hadron correlation data to evaluate jet-medium interactions for 200 GeV $Au+Au$, $d+Au$ collisions. The data were studied across various transverse momentum thresholds, rapidity settings, and central $d+Au$ collisions. The observed hadron suppression in the photon-hadron data was consistent with the partonic energy loss predictions in a quark-gluon plasma. The hadron-to-photon $P_T$ spectra shape deviation from $Au+Au$ data was linked to the hadron's interaction with the medium, influenced by the energy loss and transport properties of the quark-gluon plasma. Moreover, the observation of a hadron enhancement in direct photon data was explained by a hadron pick-up process, facilitated by the medium and supported by $d+Au$ collisions.

In this study, we analyze the Smarandache's sigma product data for various geometric shapes, including prime numbers, squares, triangles, and five-sided polygons. Additionally, we determine the universal formulas for their Smarandache's sigma products.

This paper delves into the limitations of using cloud-based data centers for compute-intensive tasks, specifically sound synthesis applications. Although cloud providers guarantee network bandwidth, real-world network conditions can be affected by unexpected fluctuations in network performance, potentially affecting application scalability. To investigate this, we conducted a large-scale empirical study using Amazon EC2 instances and developed a fault-tolerant, load-balanced application called Sound in the Clouds. Our findings reveal that while the application can scale to a few hundred concurrent users, a sudden increase in load can cause a cascade of failures due to unexpected task migrations. To address this issue, we propose a simple load-shaping policy that smooths out traffic and enables the application to handle over 8000 concurrent users with minimal task migration. Our work highlights the importance of accounting for real-world network conditions when designing scalable cloud applications and could inform similar designs for other network-sensitive cloud services.

In a context-sensitive decision-making framework, agents can enhance their knowledge by making choices that are linked to specific indicators, which vary according to circumstances. We examine how agents can learn from their decisions when there are no limits on the size of these indicators and the agents do not have access to their neighbors' contexts. We demonstrate that context-independent learning can be achieved with only a minimal loss of performance compared to learning that takes into account the agents' contexts, and this is done for both loss functions that are strongly convex and those that are convex, and for both noise-free and noisy scenarios, and we also investigate the effect of the agents' contexts on the rate at which learning occurs.

In today's diverse and distributed workforces, agile methodology is highly sought after and is being utilized in a wide range of organizations.
Despite its widespread adoption, there is still a significant knowledge gap concerning the dynamics of multi-team agile projects, and in particular, there is a pressing need to identify and address any issues that may arise from telecommuting in such projects.
This research fills that gap by exploring how telecommuting impacts organizations that are managing multi-team Scrum projects, and it does so through a multi-phase approach.
We begin by examining the prevalence of telecommuting in such projects and then move on to a series of empirical studies to uncover the issues that telecommuters face when working on multi-Scrum projects.
Finally, we combine our empirical findings with input from practitioners to provide practical advice on how to overcome these issues and ensure the success of multi-Scrum projects.
Our multi-Method approach is unique in its ability to bridge the theoretical and applied aspects of multi-Scrum projects and it does so by integrating the insights of managers, practitioners and professionals with extensive experience in such projects.

We appreciate the interest shown by Kang, Lee, and Suh in our research. In response to their commentary, we reiterate that our primary objective was to empirically assess the performance of our proposed DRL solution in JOINT through open-source software, which is not feasible given the scale of national healthcare datasets used by Kang, Lee, and Suh. As the supplementary material and Section 7 of our manuscript indicate, we have already addressed the concerns regarding the causality assumption, sample size limitations, and distributional assumption in our model. Furthermore, given the complexity of real-world clinical settings, it is challenging to completely specify the distribution in KOS, which is why our proposed DRL method in JOINT is more adaptable. Finally, our JOINT model can also incorporate the elements discussed by Kang, Lee, and Suh in their KOS approach.

This analysis examines the connection between geometric distortions and initial arrangements in lead-lead collisions at 2.76 TeV, focusing on how final particle motions relate to geometric fluctuations. A method is used to evaluate the average and fluctuations of the event shape and orientation, divided into quadrupoles based on a specific transverse momentum range. It is found that the average shape fluctuates significantly and that fluctuations in orientation are minimal. Notably, events with similar orientation distributions have different particle charge patterns. An examination of elliptic fluctuations using a specific observable called $v_{22}$ reveals that particles with similar momenta do not always move in similar paths, especially for lower masses. This examination also includes an assessment of data accuracy and further analysis will be conducted with improved accuracy.

This paper introduces a novel class of anti-unitary operators, specifically tailored to the Quaternion Linear Canonical S Transform (QCLES), which facilitates a streamlined derivation of the Robertson-Schr\"{o}dinger uncertainty principle for quaternions. We leverage this transform to obtain an explicit form of the Schr\"{o}dinger uncertainty equality, and demonstrate its connection to an optimal representation within the QCLES domain. Additionally, the paper expands upon both the basic and advanced properties of the QCLES transform, and introduces novel time-frequency bounds related to the $L^p$ norms of signals and their QCLES transforms, which can be applied in the context of signal reconstruction.

The extremal GDoF advantage of employing an optimal power regulation scheme over a binary power regulation method in a $K$ user symmetric interference network is $\Theta(\sqrt{K})$. Findings from previous events indicate that when users have unlimited power availability, the benefit of implementing optimal power regulation is enhanced. Conversely, when power resources are constrained, research indicates that binary power regulation is sufficient. This investigation fills the gap between these two extremes by determining the GDoF advantage of optimal power regulation as a function of power resources available. Our results reveal that binary power regulation is sufficient for achieving maximum GDoF benefits when power resources are of a certain order, whereas when power resources are either significantly greater or considerably lesser than this threshold, there is an appreciable GDoF advantage to be gained from employing an optimal power regulation scheme.

In particle-resolved simulations for complex multiphase systems, a significant computational burden arises due to calculating the matrix inversion for colliding particles, which can be circumvented by employing a physically realistic collision duration. Instead of treating this as an instantaneous event, we consider it duration-based, allowing us to decouple this matrix computation from the time-scale of fluid integration. A novel multi-time-step integration scheme is thus developed, and its effectiveness is demonstrated through various test cases, including particle clustering and coexistence of monolayers, fluidization of beds, and the formation of particle shells, when compared to traditionally used methods.

This article will examine the equation $a^2+ab+b^2=7^n$ in detail, offering proven insights for multiple whole number conditions on $n$. We will establish a correspondence between the number of whole number solutions and the number of non-negative whole number solutions of the equation $7r^2-2^s-2^t=0$, where 'r' is a positive whole number. Additionally, this examination will provide a distinguishing criterion for whole number solutions of $(a,b)$ and non-negative whole number solutions of $(r,s,t)$, ultimately showing that there are exactly $2^{n-3}$ whole number solutions of $(a,b)$ for specified conditions on 'n'.

This paper presents an innovative approach to modeling a single-legged hopping robot operating on a viscoelastic surface. It involves developing a simplified surface model and verifying its accuracy through surface deformation measurements during a hopping simulation. The simulation was designed to mirror the robot's movement dynamics and was subsequently modified by incorporating a control algorithm based on reinforcement learning. Results demonstrate that the robot can successfully learn to navigate the simulated environment and are discussed from both robotic and modeling perspectives.

Within a unified framework, we derive predictions for elastic meson form factors, specifically $\pi^\pm$, $K^\pm$, and $B^\pm$ mesons, by applying the relativistic random phase approximation at the relativistic level. Initially, the RPA includes relativistic effects and then extends to the relativistic Bloch-Hore path integral approach for calculations. Notably, B-meson calculations are performed within a confined quark model framework, yielding consistent results with the RPA and BHI. The RPA and BH yield distinct outcomes, yet both can be related through specific parameters, showing similar behavior in the low $Q^2$ momentum regime. The findings are supported by available experimental data, illustrating the framework's reliability in predicting meson elasticity properties.

A notable self-sustaining oscillation phenomenon, the droplet electrohydrodynamic fan, has been exhibited for the initial time using a periodically adjusted DC voltage. A specially designed, adaptable electrode system allows for easier reproduction of this system's performance. An intricate mathematical model was created to replicate the observed behavior, and according to the model's steady-state settings, the droplet's surface tension can be divided into two components, with one influenced by voltage following a $V^2$ pattern. By leveraging the model's parameter adjustment features, the mechanism behind the droplet's fan-like motion was elucidated. Specifically, it was established that friction caused by the electrode and the droplet's weight can be surpassed by reduced surface tension when a certain voltage threshold is met. Furthermore, detailed analysis of the system's dynamics, including periodic and unpredictable movements, was accomplished using various dynamical indicators as the voltage was varied. The occurrence of exhibition in this study was confirmed through experimental verification of bifurcation and coexistence of attractors patterns. Additionally, the influence of fluid properties and electrode geometry on the occurrence of exhibition was explored.

When discussing changes, it's often necessary to distinguish between similar entities and comprehend negation. Studies have shown that the prefrontal cortex, a brain region, handles both similar memory and negation. Nevertheless, existing negation tests do not test similarity, making it difficult to establish a link between the two. To bridge this gap, we created CONDAQA, a new set of 1,388 questions that are based on natural language descriptions of objects within boxes and focus on negation and categorization. Our analyses revealed that models lacking neural pretraining on the CONDAQA dataset struggle with negation, but excel when comparing equal entities. Furthermore, we discovered that both the distillation dataset and models which undergo both comparative and negational training, show an fMRI-matched profile when examined with the fMRI study on the prefrontal cortex. This finding indicates that a neural network is capable of mapping its activities to those of the human brain, and that both categories are necessary for understanding negation.

Discovering and representing the underlying framework of complex, multi-dimensional data is an age-old yet continually relevant challenge. Whether uncovering underlying patterns in social networks or analyzing financial markets, understanding the structure of information is paramount for effective decision-making. Statistical and machine learning techniques are often employed to identify latent structures, but their complex nature can hinder clear communication. To bridge this gap, graph-based methods offer a straightforward and effective supplementary approach, complementing statistical findings with visual representations of underlying relationships. In this paper, we explore contemporary scalable scalable frameworks for detecting graph structures, highlighting their potential for communicating the intricate connections within high-dimensional data.

A proposed exact cover solver, designed for a quantum annealing optimizer or simulator, is introduced in this study. We analyze its performance under various test conditions and verify results through a conventional approach. According to our findings, certain dynamics crucial to understanding quenching can be examined by varying specific parameters. These include studying the impact of initial state quenching on the system's final state distribution and the influence of the annealing interval on the system's state, particularly in the post-quench phase. Notably, certain states can be reached more efficiently by adjusting the release time of the system's evolution.

To ensure safety systems function correctly, model checking is commonly used with formal specifications like temporal logic. However, the corrections following a failed verification can be difficult to apply in real-world scenarios. This study aims to provide a method for checking the compliance of three-party transactions with formal models by using information system traces. The process involves aligning partial futures after the transaction and at other points in time. The proposed method allows for the identification of discrepancies between the actual process and the expected outcome, as well as the identification of any deviations from the expected process. The method is applied to a transaction-based information system.

To determine the screening strength, we apply both Slater and Hund's rules within a spin-charge separation framework, considering Ginzburg-Landau theories of superconductivity. Our analysis indicates that screening influences superconducting gap equations and, ultimately, the critical temperature. We verify our findings by comparing them to calculations within the dual-band model of infinite-layer nickelate.

This paper addresses the long-term behavior of the non-cutoff Boltzmann equation in three-dimensional space, focusing on small perturbations around a equilibrium state and hard potentials without attraction forces. We have established a phase blending theory for the non-cutoff equation that mirrors a fundamental concept in fluid dynamics where distinct fluids intermingle. By integrating this theory with an existing result for Landau equation, we have derived a precise exponential decay rate for solutions to the non-cutoff Boltzmann equation. Additionally, we have established corresponding bounds for solutions to the kinetic fractional equation with a fractional Laplacian.

We re-examine the Cox and Munk wave-tilt statistics using radiance measurements of the ocean surface obtained from the IASI instrument aboard the EUMETSAT meteorological satellite. By analyzing a satellite image of the ocean surface, we determine directional wave variances at specific wavelengths, in this case 3.7 and 6.2 um. After accounting for the satellite's viewing angle, we derive normal and planar wave variances. Our results show that the derived statistics match the predictions of Cox and Munk within the range of 30 cm/s^2 to 60 cm/s^2. Additionally, our research indicates that the difference between normal and planar wave variances can be used to determine the direction of the prevailing wind. The difference is maximized when the wind is吹着 the satellite's sensor and the effect diminishes as the satellite moves away from the wind direction.

When a software product is released, user feedback often leads to the need for additional features, which can lengthen the time from planning to release. One effective way to gather user opinions is through app stores, but the process of adding new features can be lengthy due to the constraint of testing all new and existing functionality. A group of developers has created a tool to speed up the process of testing all combinations of software in a specific environment by focusing on two key aspects. The tool first identifies frequently co-used features in the environment and then uses a algorithm to find the smallest set of 应用 that can cover the tested new and existing features. A preliminary evaluation of the algorithm has demonstrated its capability to reduce the search time for optimal solutions, but the process is still time-consuming for a single computer, particularly with a larger number of aspects. In an effort to overcome this limitation, a method has been proposed to parallelize the test case selection process on multiple computers, thereby allowing for a broader range of environment analyses.

This research involves a large collection of Chinese microblog posts related to the Coronavirus pandemic, allowing for an exploration of public sentiment and emotional responses during this period. A total of 1.44 million data samples were manually categorized into six emotional classes – anger, fear, sadness, empathy, skepticism, and neutrality – and analyzed to extract meaningful insights. A sentiment classification model based on Bayesian networks was developed and validated, achieving a 71.5% accuracy in determining public sentiment and emotional outcomes. The results of this study can be used to support the design of targeted public health messaging, and may also be applicable to similar events worldwide.

Integrating all available experimental evidence, a two-liquid model has been proposed for cuprate superconductors. This model involves an spin-carrying superatomic conduction electron liquid and an magnetic-shearing Cu-O dimer conduction hole liquid, existing as interlayer coupled Haldane topological insulator domains. We demonstrate that this model generalizes previous interlayer conduction models and can be mathematically expressed using Fermi-Dirac and Landau equations modified to account for the topological insulator nature, combined with 1D soliton equations that describe the interaction between the two liquids. As a result, we can derive the observed cuprate phenomenology, including the two-peak ARPES spectra, linear in-plane resistivity, and the Neel edge of the antiferromagnetic phase, while also being able to predict the critical temperature for topological transition.

Research into very dense matter within the cores of neutron stars has revealed that sound speed data may provide insights into the nature of this matter. Specifically, the finding that sound speed approaches one third the speed of light in some density ranges conflicts with observed neutron star properties. However, recent research indicating the existence of compact stars with masses over two solar masses implies very high central densities. This could mean the sound speed constraint applies to a smaller portion of the matter density profile, not limiting the existence of certain equation of state models. Furthermore, the ultimate fate of massive stars under gravitational influence, specifically whether they become black holes or strange stars, could depend on the sound speed in dense matter, with some equations of state precluding the formation of strange stars.

The analysis of unordered, labeled phylogenies is typically hindered by an uneven distribution of area codes when mapping to specific characters, which can compromise the sensitivity to relevant features. A novel approach, known as adverse tai mapping, is introduced to address this challenge, enabling the phylogenies to be mapped onto the target space in a way that is both balanced and meaningful, which can improve the performance of learning phylogenies from sequential data.

We examine how deformation affects both discrete and continuous position-momentum modes in state representations, specifically looking at the impact of squeezing and shift on the Fock space. Building on the 1989 compass state formulation, we introduce deformed annihilation and creation operators that lower and raise deformed number states by one and two states respectively. We derive the annihilation and creation operators for both position-momentum Susskind-Glogower and the deformed Smorodinsky type ladders, specifically showing that our new operators can be linked to the Susskind-Glogower and Smorodinsky type ladders under specific conditions, i.e., no deformation or second-order deformation only.

A vertical shearing instability arises when a disk's viscosity is influenced by a decrease in shear stress due to an increase in temperature. By simulating a two-dimensional interaction between dust and gas under conditions of VSI development in a disk at 10 AU, it was found that the accretion of the gas is amplified due to an increase in the Spitzer viscosity as a result of dust heating above the point where they are coupled with the gas. This results in the formation of a temperature peak without dust and the subsequent development of turbulent mixing that leads to the formation of a temperature gradient that is conducive to the development of the VSI. In contrast, in a disk at 0.7 AU, it was found that the average temperature of dust increases due to their interaction and this leads to an increase in the Spitzer viscosity of the gas and this leads to an outflow of the gas and the formation of a temperature peak without dust and the subsequent development of turbulent mixing that leads to the formation of a temperature gradient that is conducive to the development of the VSI. However, in a disk at 0.05 AU, it was found that the average temperature of dust increases due to their interaction and this leads to an increase in the Spitzer viscosity of the gas and this leads to an outflow of the gas and the formation of a temperature peak without dust and the subsequent development of turbulent mixing that leads to the formation of a temperature gradient that is conducive to the development of the

This paper explores the consequences of a recent result by the authors concerning complete, non-compact manifolds with a constant Ricci curvature. It is demonstrated that if such a manifold has a non-zero average scalar curvature and is covered by a 'diminutor' field, then it must be covered by a complete gradient Ricci soliton. Following this, the paper proves that any such diminutor field is actually a complete gradient scalar Ricci soliton when the manifold's average scalar curvature is constant. As a consequence, we obtain a new proof for a result by N. Troncoli on the equivalence between certain types of diminutor fields and complete gradient Ricci soliton fields under the condition of a constant scalar curvature.

Recently, Conditional Generative Adversarial Networks have excelled in conditioned image generation, particularly in tasks involving single-digit conditions. However, their capability to manage multi-digit conditions or conditions that span diverse semantic domains remains limited. To address this issue, we introduce a novel approach called Dynamic Entrezones with Global Mean Pooling, or ZE-GMP, which enhances the handling of four-digit conditions and conditions across diverse semantic domains. By integrating a conditional embedding mechanism that processes multi-digit conditions using embedding sum, and controlling the latent distribution through dynamic entrances, we present a robust framework for conditional generation. Our approach has been tested on the MNIST and CMU-ART datasets and demonstrates superior performance compared to existing methods, particularly in handling multi-digit conditions and conditions that span diverse semantic domains.

The influence of post-Newtonian gravity on modern-day and Gaia-like astrometry is being re-evaluated, with a focus on how the PPN parameter gamma affects the measurement of parallaxes, proper motions, and the overall $\delta \chi^2$ in the Gaia data. As the accuracy of satellite astrometry improves, the data will in the future be more sensitive to relativistic effects, potentially allowing for the determination of key parameters like the PPN parameter gamma from the data itself. Moreover, the variability of solar gravitational influences on parallax variability and the proposed approach of incorporating a rank-2 tensor term in the Baïcon code to avoid the bias of proper motion estimates caused by the unaccounted parallax variability are also examined. The study finds that the unaddressed post-Newtonian effects result in a $\delta \chi^2$ of around 0.15 for the Gaia data, a negligible impact of curvature and semi-major axis variations of the light cones of the solar gravitational influence on the parallax variability, and the impact of the unmodeled variation on the global $\delta \chi^2$, the precision of parallax $\sigma_\varpi$, and proper motion $\sigma_\mu$ estimates for the Gaia $\beta$ and $\delta \chi^2$ metrics.

Complex systems such as chemical reactions, neural networks, and economic models are commonly modeled using high-dimensional nonlinear dynamical systems.
Despite the wealth of information that these models provide, their sheer complexity often hinders effective analysis and control due to the difficulty of working with a large number of state variables.
In an effort to address this challenge, we have developed a novel approach that utilizes data to quickly generate a simplified model capable of accurately capturing the essential behavior of the underlying system.
By applying techniques for dimensionality reduction, our approach simultaneously identifies a lower-dimensional subspace and projects the system's dynamics onto it, resulting in a significantly smaller number of state variables.
We have demonstrated our method's effectiveness by rapidly reducing the complexity of a chemical reaction system and a chemical neural network, achieving a substantial reduction in the number of state variables within a short period of time.
Our approach opens up new possibilities for the real-time analysis and effective design of control systems for complex dynamics.

A well-known feature of lower-dimensional systems is spontaneous current generation, which can be observed in the form of magnetization in polymers or spin waves in films, typically requiring an external power. Contrary to this, we have discovered a self-sustained current in a one-component Bose-Einstein condensate that does not break up and creates self-localized dark-bright structures. These structures, which consist of two interacting parts, generate opposite currents in each component and become self-trapped as a result of the mean-field effect. Notably, these structures can support multiple modes of oscillation, where they exchange energy with an external pump and recover their initial state, demonstrating robustness. This work paves the way for stable multi-mode states with self-generated interactions in BEC systems.

This research addresses the challenge of protecting machine learning (ML) model usage in a scenario where a legitimate user employs a machine learning model that has been trained by a skilled trainer but is hosted on a machine that has been taken over by a malicious actor. This malicious actor attempts to manipulate the model with input data that has been secretly modified. To achieve this, we first introduce a straightforward and straightforward method, SIMC, that is capable of preventing unauthorized modification of the machine that has been compromised. SIMC is composed of a verification module, that is, a secret-sharing technique, and a security module, that is, a random encoding, which is designed to prevent the malicious actor from accessing the machine learning (ML) model. We have evaluated the performance of SIMC, and found that it effectively resists multiple types of attacks, including those involving a machine learning model with multiple neural networks. In addition, we have made the code for SIMC available to other researchers at the following link: https://github.com/hkdw2/Secure-ML-Inference.

The radio telescope known as FAST has a powerful sensitivity that is ideal for a thorough exploration of the 21-cm hydrogen emission and absorption features throughout the entire electromagnetic spectrum. A set of observations centered on the M101 galaxy and its surrounding group, have yielded a rich collection of hydrogen lines, including within the first group of galaxies. Notably, a significant portion of these lines were unassigned in previous observations. A close examination of their properties, including position, motion, and motion paths, led to the conclusion that these lines could be attributed to dark matter halos. A hydrogen tail was also found associated with M101. This discovery could be attributed to tidal forces caused by M101's motion. This is a significant breakthrough as it marks the first instance of a hydrogen cloud being found within a galaxy group, as well as the first time a hydrogen tail was found associated with a spiral galaxy using a very sensitive observation. This finding also highlights the need to update and refine our understanding of how galaxies, and their hydrogen components, interact with each other.

Effectively tackling Open-Domain Question-Answering (ODQA) is severely hampered by a lack of detailed world knowledge. To bridge this gap, we propose a COre SemANTic-graph (COSENA) that integrates diverse entities and their interconnections to expand the COSENA's semantic understanding of the world. Although COSENA provides a broad foundation for answering questions, it is COSENA's COarse- to Precise (CP) mechanism that enables a deep analysis of COSENA's semantic-related insight, enabling a tailored graph structure to efficiently find the most relevant evidence to answer questions. Our experiments reveal that COSENA outperforms existing ODSA baselines on the CommonsenseQA and SocialQA benchmarks, outdoing them by up to 6.1 F1 on average. Moreover, COSENA's COarse-to-Precise (CP) module demonstrates its ability to refine COSENA's semantic-related insight to enable a more precise ODQA. To illustrate our points, we provide a concrete example in Figure 1 that shows how COSENA's COarse-to-Precise (CP) graph is more relevant to the question than the COSENA's COre SemANTic-graph (COSENA).

The presence of compounds containing Carbon, Hydrogen and Oxygen in the comets has been observed through analysis of the cometary coma and tail, although a complete understanding of the chemical processes at work in comets is still lacking due to, in part, limitations in current databases describing the spectra of oxygen-containing molecules found in comets. A comprehensive survey of existing cometary database discovered a significant gap in our knowledge of these molecules with molecules comprising Carbon dimer molecules were found to be significantly underrepresented in terms of available spectral data. This in turn means that the identification of these molecules in comets is in many cases doubtful due to the possibility that unaccounted spectral features may be responsible for previous observations indicating the presence of these molecules. This issue means that in order to accurately identify the cometary composition, new and more detailed spectral data of cometary molecules is required in order to prevent the misinterpretation of observational data obtained from comets.

The problem of representing a global element as a sum of non-negative squares has long been studied in the context of real and p-adic numbers, as well as in the context of expressing a global field element as a sum of non-negative squares. While it is always possible to express an element from any global field as a sum of four squares due to a well-known theorem by Hasse-Minkowski, the critical issue lies in determining the smallest number of non-negative squares (i.e., the constant $s$) needed to represent a general element from specific global fields such as $\mathbb{Q}$, $\mathbb{Q}_p$, and specific number fields and function fields. A recent breakthrough has been made in this area, as the authors of the paper have recently demonstrated that any rational number can be represented as the sum of three non-negative squares and in this work, they aim to build upon this by addressing the same problem in a broader context, specifically within $\mathbb{Q}_p$, certain $p$-adic fields, and direct products of these fields, as well as certain number fields and function fields over finite fields.

The vast amount of data produced by modern spectral surveys makes it nearly
impossible for a single researcher to analyze effectively. Although a technique
we call astrophotonic crossmatching has been developed to help researchers
combine different datasets, the increasing number of data products will quickly
outstrip the capacity of human researchers to manually combine these datasets.
This introduction outlines the principles behind the astrophotonic crossmatching
technique and the tools we have created to facilitate this process, before
detailing its features in subsequent sections of our paper. As a case study, we
examine the use of the astrophotonic crossmatching technique with the observations
from the high-resolution APOGEE and NIRSPEC-MSTIS surveys, showcasing the
capabilities of the method. To address the challenge of spectral inconsistencies
between different datasets due to variations in spectral resolution and signal-to-noise
ratio, we propose a pair of innovative strategies known as photonic-merge and
photonic-match. These innovations represent an advancement in the field of
crossmatching, allowing for a more seamless combination of spectral and photometric
data sets regardless of the quality of the spectra involved.

Medication Pair Prediction is a crucial task with significant implications for Accelerated Approval New Drug Indications and Identifying Effective Drug-Drug Combinations. This study presents a cohesive perspective on Relational Deep Learning applications to Medication Pair Prediction, beginning with an examination of various embedding representations used in this context. A novel representation, the Graph Representation, is introduced, and its performance is evaluated against state-of-the-art approaches. Findings reveal that the Graph Representation, in conjunction with specific relational learning techniques, leads to more efficient and accurate models, as demonstrated by implementations using dropout and negative sampling, and the model's robustness is further explored through sensitivity analysis.

Consider a time-varying transformation $\Phi(t,x)$ that creates a moving boundary $\Omega_t = \Phi(t, \mathbb{T}^d)$, where the transformation is considered to be rough in the time dimension. Assuming the transformation satisfies a suitable regularity and non-degeneracy conditions, and given sources $f$ and $g$ along with initial data $u_0$, we define $u$ as the solution to the problem that involves finding a function $u \in H^1( \bigg( \bigg( 0, T \bigg) \times \mathbb{T}^d \bigg) , \bigg| _{\partial \bigg( (0,T) \times \mathbb{T}^d \bigg)} ^{\partial_\tau + P_\ast \beta \cdot \partial_x }$ such that $u$ satisfies the conditions $u(\tau, \cdot) \in \Omega_\tau$, $u_0 = u(0, \cdot)$, and the equation $\partial_\tau u + \Delta_x u = f$ holds almost everywhere in $(0,T) \times \mathbb{T}^d$, and $\partial_\tau u + \beta \cdot \partial_x u = g$ holds almost everywhere in $\big

A Federated Learning setup that includes a single large model and a smaller group of contributing clients is often unfair, as it's similar to a cloud learning scenario where a large pre-trained model is fine-tuned by a small group. To prevent the model from deviating from the contributing users' classes in this model, we've proposed a new approach to FL called Random Stroll Learning (FedStroll). This approach introduces a stochastic element to the FL process. We've developed a specialized Stroll loss that guides the model to perform an "idle walk" while taking each client's input. The FedStroll approach incorporates this technique into the standard FL training cycle. We've demonstrated its effectiveness in a regular FL setting and a scenario with a single large model and a small group of contributing users. Our experiments show that FedStroll leads to more reliable and consistent results.

This research provides a computational verification of the initial inertial wave turbulence theory. Despite its straightforward formulation, the model provides an idealized and highly scalable scenario for observing the cascade of energy across inertial waves. By employing a high-performance computing system, the researchers simulated a wide range of scales, and compared simulated spectra to predicted T4 and T5 laws. These agreements are obtained for moderate levels of forced energy.

This research focuses on enhancing the criminal justice system by incorporating mental wellness considerations, specifically examining the positive influence of court-mandated mental health and substance abuse treatment for inmates. A dataset from the California Superior Court in Los Angeles, spanning 2004 to 2010, is used to analyze recidivism rates among defendants with and without mental health issues, taking into account whether they received treatment. The study's findings show that mental health problems can increase recidivism rates, but this increase is countered when the individuals receive treatment, particularly for those committing property crimes. These results highlight the potential of the court system to improve mental wellness and reduce future criminal behavior through mandated treatment.
A widely used and effective method for consistency regularization in semi-supervised medical image segmentation is known as the 3D UNet approach.

The ATLAS Jet Trigger System on the ATLAS detector at the LHC needs to process a vast amount of data supplied by the Calorimeter (TFC) and efficiently identify significant jets. To cope with the high data rates anticipated at LHC Run 3, upgrading the TFC system is necessary. One key component of the ATLAS TFC system is the Jet Filter Circuit (JFC), responsible for identifying significant jets among the many candidates provided by the TFC. We present a novel design for the JFC that leverages two ATTRA 7T FPGA chips and UltraScale+ architecture to process data at a rate of 500 Terabytes per second and handle an input of 720 GBits per second. With 54,720 logic elements available, the new design can identify significant jets above the 950 Gibits per second threshold with a latency of 63 clock cycles operating at a 42 MHz frequency.

In the field of Computer Graphics and Virtual Reality, creating lifelike 3D human avatars that can express a wide range of emotions and movements is a significant challenge.  A crucial aspect of this challenge involves accurately representing joint rotations, as errors in this area can cause noticeable discrepancies in avatar movement and facial expressions. To address this issue, we present ANR, a framework based on conditional normalizing flows that allows for the realistic visualization of articulated 3D human bodies. ANR can reconstruct complex poses from single images and expresses emotions through blended shape and motion components conditioned on retargeting masks. Evaluations using public datasets demonstrate that ANR outperforms existing methods in terms of pose accuracy and overall quality.

Controlling and predicting the erratic behavior of chaotic systems is essential in a variety of fields, including fluid dynamics, weather forecasting, and quantum chaos. We have developed a novel machine learning algorithm, ChaoNet, to accurately model complex chaotic dynamics. ChaoNet, a type of graph neural network, can be interpreted to provide insights into the mechanisms of chaos control. We have demonstrated the effectiveness of ChaoNet by applying it to a chaotic laser system, allowing us to successfully regulate the unwanted erratic behavior of the system through precise control of a chemical component. The ChaoNet framework may have significant implications for the development of more efficient ways to manage chaotic systems in areas where such control is critical, such as weather modification.

Consider $X_1, \dots, X_n$ as independent and identically distributed variables, with a known distribution $F$ that depends on an unknown parameter $\theta$. The goal is to estimate the distribution's characteristic function $\mu = E[g(X)]$, where $g$ is a given function and the expectation $\mu$ can be expressed as $E[g(\theta)]$. Alternatively, estimating $\mu$ can be approached by directly estimating $g(X_i)$ for $i = 1, \dots, n$ and then using the average of these estimates. This paper investigates an alternative, more efficient method to achieve this objective, by analyzing the likelihood of a generalized model and showing that, under specific regularity conditions, the resulting estimator consistently estimates $\mu$ and normally converges at a rate of $n^{1/2}$. The performance of this estimator is then evaluated, along with Generalized Maximum Likelihood (GML) and traditional likelihood methods, through numerical simulations.

As searching and reading vast online content becomes increasingly unmanageable for humans, it is crucial to present relevant information in a comprehensible format. Velez and Gonzalez proposed the concept of "knowledge tracing" to track the evolving understanding of an online content viewer or listener. Various machine learning methods, particularly deep learning-based models like pyNTLM, have been developed to create tracing markers that indicate points of significant content. To evaluate such models, we need a Python library with consistent and reliable evaluation metrics. In this paper, we present pyKT, a Python library that facilitates the evaluation of knowledge tracing models by providing a unified interface and ensuring reproducibility across different evaluation methods and setups.

This study proves that for any infinite-dimensional subset within a space of smooth functions on a compact manifold, the closure of that subset in the $C^\infty$ topology contains an elliptic operator, and under certain conditions, contains a maximal elliptic operator. These findings lead to a revised and improved version of a previous argument, demonstrating that the closure of any infinite-dimensional subset in $C^\infty(M)$ contains a maximal elliptic operator for a specific type of manifold.

This paper introduces Alethe, a high-level language for structuring SMT proofs, along with a corresponding verifier to facilitate proof analysis and modification. The design of Alethe takes into account the diverse proof formats producible by various solvers and checks for compliance with specific criteria. The concepts presented in our work have been adopted by several projects, including Coq's Theorem Prover Interoperability (TPV) framework, Lean's extraction and refinement mechanisms, and Isabelle's automated proof components in the Fourier, Ssreflect, and Equations libraries.

This paper focuses on the widespread use of federated learning in its various applications. Although it has been successfully utilized in multiple settings, researchers have been unable to experiment with the technique due to lacking a standardized benchmark for evaluation. This project aims to provide the first standardized benchmark for evaluating and researching federated learning. It also introduces a reference implementation and results demonstrating the effectiveness of buffer-based, asynchronous, and unconstrained gradient aggregation methods. These results suggest that methods with unconstrained aggregation can converge at rates comparable to other well-established optimization techniques.

We've reviewed the current ASner ASR technology and found that it's based on a particular training approach, fine-tuning, that uses a training model of human handwriting and a higher-res model for actual data. Our study examined whether this resolution-based transfer can be applied to automatic speech recognition (ASR) without utilizing a human-generated model. We've conducted an in-depth analysis of the ASner system and identified the challenges in replicating it. Furthermore, we've explored whether training the ASR model directly on low-quality data, created from distorted clean samples, could produce the same results. We've conducted experiments with both approaches, using cepstrum and mel-spectrograms as audio features. Our findings indicate that directly modeling the production process of poor audio quality from clean speech is more effective than simply transferring the resolution of drawings or recordings. To support other researchers in this area, we've made the ASner code and our experimental data available online.

The complexity of graph representation learning is attributed to two proximity concepts: structural role and topological distance. A comprehensive and diverse real-world graph dataset is required to evaluate representation methods that preserve both aspects of proximity. We introduce Twitch Players, a medium-sized graph between 500 KB and 1 MB in size, focused on social network relationships. This dataset, collected from Twitch.tv, represents familial ties within the community. We provide a thorough examination of 200 distinct features describing subgraphs extracted from the overall graph. This examination includes the application of over 100 unique node embedding techniques, resulting in a set of diverse and rich data sets that correspond to specific proximity concepts.

Our analysis focuses on the $1450< t < 1500$ mass gap, employing LHCb data from $B^0\to \pi^+\pi^-$, $B^0\to K^+K^-$, $B^0\to K^+K^-$ ($S$-wave) and $B^0\to K_S K^+$ $\rho^0\to \pi^+\pi^-$ decay modes to examine the structure of the $1420< t < 1490$ interval. While previous studies found the $f_2(1420)$ and $f_2(1500)$ resonances in $B^0\to \pi^+\pi^-$ decays, they reported only a broad enhancement in the corresponding channels for $B^0\to K^+K^-$ and $B^0\to K_S K^+$ $\rho^0\to \pi^+\pi^-$ decays.
